unit.title: Use and maintain graduated measuring devices

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a "graduated" measuring device?
options: A tool that is only used by trainees who have graduated
A tool that has no markings and is set by eye
A tool used only to check that a surface is level
A tool marked with a scale of equal divisions

questions.stem: Which tool is best for measuring the length of a 6 m steel bar or a long cable run?
options: A steel tape measure
A micrometer
A vernier caliper
A 300 mm steel rule

questions.stem: Which tool would you use to measure the thickness of a 3 mm sheet to 0.01 mm?
options: A steel tape measure with a hook
A 1 m wooden rule
An outside micrometer
A spirit level

questions.stem: Which tool can measure an outside size, an inside size and a depth?
options: An outside micrometer
A vernier caliper
A steel tape measure
A try square

questions.stem: What is the smallest division on most metric steel rules used in the workshop?
options: 1 cm (10 mm) only
0.5 mm or 1 mm
0.01 mm or 0.02 mm
5 mm or 10 mm

questions.stem: Why is it often better to measure from the 10 mm mark rather than the very end of a steel rule?
options: The end of the rule is always marked in inches
The numbers right at the end are much too small to read
The end may be worn, which gives a wrong reading
Rules are only accurate in the middle third

questions.stem: Why does the hook on the end of a tape measure move a little?
options: So that inside and outside readings both start at true zero
Because it has worked loose, and the tape must be replaced
So that the blade can be wound back into the case faster
To stop the steel blade from rusting in damp weather

questions.stem: How should you look at a scale to avoid "parallax error"?
options: From one side, at an angle of about 45°
From as far away as you can manage
With one eye shut and the other eye looking from the side
With your eye straight in line with the mark

questions.stem: On a metric vernier caliper, which part gives the fine reading?
options: The vernier scale on the sliding jaw
The main scale on the beam
The locking screw on the top of the sliding jaw
The depth rod at the end

questions.stem: Many metric vernier calipers can read to how fine a measurement?
options: 1.0 mm
0.5 mm

questions.stem: A vernier caliper's main scale shows 24 mm before the vernier zero, and the 7th vernier line (0.02 mm each) lines up. What is the reading?
Which part of a vernier caliper is used to measure the depth of a hole?
options: The outside jaws
The inside jaws
The depth rod
The thumb wheel

questions.stem: Which part of a vernier caliper measures the inside of a pipe?
options: The depth rod at the end
The beam's main scale
The inside jaws at the top
The outside jaws at the bottom

questions.stem: On a metric micrometer, how far does the spindle move for one full turn of the thimble?
options: 1.0 mm
0.5 mm

questions.stem: A metric micrometer's thimble has 50 divisions. What is each division worth?
options: 0.1 mm
0.5 mm

questions.stem: A micrometer sleeve shows 12 mm and one 0.5 mm line after it. The thimble reads 28. What is the reading?
What is the ratchet on a micrometer for?
options: To lock the spindle so that it cannot turn at all
To set the micrometer back to zero after use
To make the spindle move faster as it gets close to the work
To give the same light pressure on every measurement

questions.stem: Which part of a micrometer is the fixed, U-shaped body?
options: The thimble
The spindle
The frame
The anvil

questions.stem: How do you check the zero on a 0–25 mm micrometer?
options: Clean the faces, close them gently with the ratchet, read 0.00
Squeeze the spindle tightly onto the anvil as hard as you possibly can
Measure a piece of paper and call that zero
Open it fully and check that the thimble reads 25

questions.stem: Why should a micrometer not be held in the hand for a long time while measuring?
options: It may slip off the work because of sweat
Body heat makes it grow slightly and reads wrong
The hand will cover up the numbers on the sleeve
It may switch itself off and lose the reading

questions.stem: Which tool is used to measure the angle of a bevel on a plate edge?
options: A steel tape measure laid on the plate
A protractor or bevel protractor
An outside micrometer
A spirit level

questions.stem: In which units are angles measured?
options: Degrees
Millimetres
Litres
Kilograms

questions.stem: What is a try square or combination square used to check?
options: That a surface is perfectly flat and level
The thickness of thin sheet metal
That two surfaces meet at 90°
The inside diameter of a pipe

questions.stem: What is meant by the "resolution" of a measuring tool?
options: How long the tool will last before it wears out
How heavy the tool is to hold and carry
The largest size that the tool can measure
The smallest change in size it can show

questions.stem: A part must be 50 mm ± 0.5 mm. Which measurement is acceptable?
What is a "tolerance" on a drawing?
options: The number of parts that must be made
The amount a size may vary and still be correct
The time allowed to finish the job
The name of the tool that must be used to measure the part

questions.stem: When marking several holes along a bar, why measure each one from the same end (a datum)?
options: So that the tape does not need to be pulled out
Because the far end of the bar is never square
So that every hole drilled comes out exactly the same size
So that small errors do not add up along the bar

questions.stem: Why should you "measure twice and cut once"?
options: Because the first reading is always wrong
To use up more time on each job
To catch a mistake before material is wasted
Because tape measures stretch after one use

questions.stem: A weld has just been made on a part. When should you take its final measurements?
options: At once, while the metal is still hot
Before the weld has been cleaned
After it has cooled to room temperature
While it is still being quenched in water

questions.stem: Why should the part and the faces of a measuring tool be wiped clean before measuring?
options: To make the tool look new for the assessor
Because the tool's oil helps it read larger
So that the tool can be used later as a small hammer on the job
Dirt or burrs between them give a false reading

questions.stem: After using a steel rule, vernier or micrometer, what should you do?
options: Leave it on the bench ready for the next day
Wipe it clean, lightly oil it and put it in its case
Wash it in water and then leave it out in the sun to dry
Put it in your pocket with your keys and coins

questions.stem: Why should steel measuring tools be lightly oiled before storing, especially in Jamaica's damp, salty air?
options: To stop rust, which can spoil the scale and moving parts
To make the scale easier to read in poor light
So that the tool slides easily into a pocket
Because a layer of oil makes the tool measure much more exactly

questions.stem: Which of these is misuse that can damage a micrometer or vernier caliper?
options: Wiping it with a clean, dry cloth
Using it as a clamp or a spanner
Keeping it in its own case
Closing it gently with the ratchet

questions.stem: You drop a vernier caliper and the jaws no longer close fully. What should you do?
options: Bend the jaws back into line with pliers
Keep using it and add a little to each reading
Stop using it, label it faulty and report it
Hide it at the back of the drawer

questions.stem: What does "calibration" of a measuring tool mean?
options: Checking it against a known standard and correcting it
Painting over the scale so that it is easier to read in poor light
Oiling the moving parts so they do not stick
Writing the owner's name on the tool

questions.stem: A micrometer's calibration sticker shows that its check date has passed. What should you do?
options: Use it, as long as the zero reading looks right to you
Peel off the sticker and use it anyway
Use it only for jobs that do not matter
Report it and use a tool that is in date

questions.stem: A tape measure has inches on one edge. About how many millimetres are 12 inches?
options: 120 mm
254 mm
305 mm

questions.stem: On a metric tape measure, how far apart are the numbered marks usually?
options: 10 mm (1 cm)
1 mm (0.1 cm)

questions.stem: An electrician measures a cable run of 7.35 m. How many millimetres is that?
options: 735 mm

questions.stem: Which tool gives the most exact outside diameter of a 20 mm conduit or a round bar?
options: A steel tape measure
A 300 mm steel rule
A vernier caliper
A try square

questions.stem: Why should measurements be written down straight away, with their units?
options: So that they are not forgotten or mixed up later
Because the tool will lose the reading after a minute
So that the assessor can see your handwriting
Because units are only needed for metric sizes

questions.stem: When measuring with a vernier caliper, how much pressure should be used on the jaws?
options: As much as possible, to get a tight grip
Light, even pressure, without forcing
None: the jaws should not touch the part
Enough to leave a mark on the part

questions.stem: Why must a tape or rule be held straight and square to the work?
options: So that the blade does not bend over and break in half
So that the reading is in millimetres
A slanted tape gives a reading that is too long
So that the numbers face the customer

questions.stem: You take an inside measurement between two walls by pressing the tape case into the corner. The case length is marked on it. What do you do?
options: Ignore the case and read the blade at the corner
Take the case length away from the blade reading
Measure twice and use the smaller reading
Add the case length marked on the case

questions.stem: Where should precision measuring tools be stored?
options: Loose in the toolbox with hammers and files
In their cases, in a clean, dry place
On the window sill in the sun
In a damp corner of the store room

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show any working. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the part of a micrometer that you turn, which has a scale marked round it?
What is the name of the fixed face of a micrometer that the work rests against, opposite the spindle?
What is the name of the screw on a vernier caliper that holds the sliding jaw so the reading does not change?
What is the name of the unit that is one thousandth (1/1000) of a metre?
How many millimetres are in one inch? Give the exact figure.
A metric micrometer's sleeve shows 7 mm with no half-millimetre line showing, and the thimble reads 15. What is the reading?
A vernier caliper's main scale reads 18 mm and the 12th vernier line lines up. Each vernier division is 0.02 mm. What is the reading?
What is the name of a hardened steel block of exact size used to check the accuracy of a micrometer or caliper?
What is the name of the long fixed bar of a vernier caliper that carries the main scale?
What is the name of the set of thin steel blades, each marked with its thickness, used to measure small gaps?
A part is drawn as 25 mm ± 0.1 mm. What is the largest size that is acceptable?
What is the name of the round, clock-faced instrument, used on a stand, that measures very small movements?
A 1 m length of flat bar is cut into 4 equal pieces (ignore the saw cut). How long is each piece in millimetres?
Which part of a micrometer moves towards the anvil to close on the work?

essays.stem: Explain how to choose the right measuring device for a job. Say when you would use a tape measure, a steel rule, a vernier caliper and a micrometer.
essays.modelAnswer: The device is chosen by the size of the item and how exact the measurement must be. The tool must be able to reach the size and must read finer than the tolerance on the drawing. A steel tape measure is used for long lengths, such as cutting a 6 m bar, marking out a gate frame or measuring a cable run, where about 1 mm is close enough. A steel rule is used for shorter lengths up to about 300 mm or 1 m, such as marking a cut on flat bar or setting a gap, reading to about 0.5 mm. A vernier caliper is used when a more exact size is needed, to about 0.02 mm, for outside sizes like a bar or conduit diameter, inside sizes like a pipe bore, and depths of holes. A micrometer is used for the most exact work, such as sheet thickness or a shaft size, reading to 0.01 mm.
markingPoints: Choose by size of item and accuracy needed (finer than the tolerance)
Tape measure for long lengths, with an example
Steel rule for shorter lengths, with an example
Vernier caliper for outside, inside and depth to about 0.02 mm
Micrometer for the most exact work, to 0.01 mm

essays.stem: Explain step by step how to take and read a measurement with a metric vernier caliper that reads to 0.02 mm.
essays.modelAnswer: First wipe the jaws and the part clean, and remove any burrs from the part. Close the jaws and check that the vernier zero lines up with the main scale zero. Open the jaws a little wider than the part, place the part well into the jaws, square to them, and close the sliding jaw gently with the thumb wheel, using light pressure. Tighten the locking screw if the caliper must be taken off the part to read it. Hold the caliper with your eye straight in line with the scale. Read the main scale at the last whole millimetre before the vernier zero, for example 32 mm. Then find the vernier line that lines up best with any main scale line, for example line 9. Multiply by 0.02: 9 × 0.02 = 0.18 mm. Add the two: 32 + 0.18 = 32.18 mm. Write it down with the unit.
markingPoints: Clean the jaws and part; check the zero
Place the part square in the jaws with light pressure; lock if needed
Read with the eye square to the scale
Main scale reading plus vernier line × 0.02
Correct worked example, written with the unit

essays.stem: Explain step by step how to take and read a measurement with a metric outside micrometer.
essays.modelAnswer: Choose a micrometer of the right range, for example 0 to 25 mm. Wipe the anvil, the spindle and the part clean. Check the zero by closing the faces gently with the ratchet: the thimble zero should line up with the line on the sleeve. Hold the micrometer by the frame, not for long, so that body heat does not change it. Open the spindle a little more than the part, place the part between the anvil and the spindle, and turn the ratchet until it clicks two or three times, so that the pressure is light and even. Lock the spindle if needed. Read the sleeve: count the whole millimetres showing, for example 8 mm, then check if a half-millimetre line is also showing, adding 0.5 mm. Then read the thimble line that meets the sleeve line, for example 37, which is 0.37 mm. Add them: 8 + 0.5 + 0.37 = 8.87 mm.
markingPoints: Right range; clean faces and part; check the zero
Use the ratchet for light, even pressure; hold by the frame briefly
Read the whole millimetres on the sleeve, plus 0.5 mm if the half line shows
Add the thimble reading in hundredths
Correct worked example

essays.stem: Describe the common causes of errors when measuring, and how to avoid each one.
essays.modelAnswer: Parallax error happens when the scale is read from an angle; avoid it by looking straight at the mark. Dirt, burrs, paint or slag on the part or on the tool's faces give a false reading; clean both first and remove burrs. Too much pressure can bend thin parts or spring the jaws; use light, even pressure and the ratchet on a micrometer. A tool that is not held square, or a tape that sags or slants, reads too long; hold it straight and square to the work. A worn or damaged tool, or one with a wrong zero, gives wrong readings; check the zero and the condition before use. Heat makes metal grow, so measure parts after they have cooled and do not hold precision tools in the hand for long. Mistakes in reading or writing are avoided by measuring twice and writing the result straight away with its unit.
markingPoints: Parallax: read square to the scale
Dirt or burrs: clean the part and the tool
Wrong pressure or tool not square: light pressure, hold straight
Worn tool or wrong zero: check before use
Heat, and reading or writing mistakes: measure cool, measure twice and record at once

essays.stem: Describe how to look after and store graduated measuring devices so that they stay accurate.
essays.modelAnswer: After use, wipe each tool clean of dust, oil, metal filings and fingerprints with a soft, clean cloth. Steel tools such as rules, squares, calipers and micrometers should be given a thin coat of light oil to stop rust, which is a real problem in Jamaica's damp, salty air. Store each tool in its own case or a padded drawer, in a clean, dry place away from heat, sunlight and heavy tools. Leave a small gap between the faces of a micrometer or caliper when storing it, and do not lock it tight. Never drop a tool, use it as a hammer, a clamp or a scriber, or force its moving parts. Do not leave a tape blade wet or let it snap back into the case. Keep the tools away from grinding and welding, where sparks and spatter can mark them. Report any damage and have tools checked and calibrated on schedule.
markingPoints: Wipe clean after use
Light oil on steel tools to stop rust
Store in cases in a clean, dry place away from heat
Do not drop, force or misuse; leave a gap between the faces
Report damage and have tools calibrated on schedule

essays.stem: Explain what calibration is, why it is needed, and what to do if a measuring device is found to be inaccurate or damaged.
essays.modelAnswer: Calibration is checking a measuring device against a standard of known size, such as a gauge block or a setting rod, to see how far its reading is out, and then adjusting it or recording the error. It is needed because tools wear, get knocked or dropped, and can go out of adjustment with use, so their readings drift. If a tool is not accurate, every part made with it may be the wrong size, which wastes material, time and money, and in electrical or structural work may make the job unsafe. Calibrated tools usually carry a label showing the date of the last check and when the next is due. If a tool is found to be inaccurate, damaged or out of date, stop using it, label it as faulty, keep it apart from good tools, report it to the supervisor or store keeper, and use another tool that is in date. Do not try to repair precision tools yourself unless trained.
markingPoints: Calibration: checking against a known standard and adjusting or recording
Needed because tools wear or get damaged and drift
Inaccurate tools cause wrong parts, waste or unsafe work
Labels show check and due dates
If faulty: stop, label, keep apart, report and use an in-date tool

essays.stem: Explain how to use a tape measure correctly for outside and inside measurements, including why the hook moves.
essays.modelAnswer: First check the tape: the blade should not be kinked or torn, the numbers should be clear, and the hook should be firm, with only its small built-in movement. For an outside measurement, such as the length of a bar, hook the end over the edge of the bar and pull the tape out straight, keeping it flat and square to the edge, and read the mark at the other end with your eye straight over it. When the hook is pulled, it slides out by its own thickness, so the reading starts from the inside face of the hook. For an inside measurement, such as between two walls, push the hook against one surface; it slides in by its own thickness, so the reading starts from its outside face. If the case is pushed into a corner, add the case length marked on it. Let the blade wind back slowly, and do not let it snap.
markingPoints: Check the blade, numbers and hook before use
Outside: hook over the edge, tape straight and square, read straight on
Hook moves by its own thickness so both readings start at true zero
Inside: push the hook against the surface, add the case length if the case is used
Let the blade wind back slowly

essays.stem: Describe the checks you should make on a measuring device before you use it.
essays.modelAnswer: First look at the tool for damage: bent jaws or blades, nicks on measuring faces, a kinked or torn tape, a loose hook, or scales that are worn and hard to read. Check that moving parts, such as the sliding jaw of a caliper or the thimble of a micrometer, move smoothly without sticking or wobbling. Wipe the measuring faces clean. Check the zero: close a caliper's jaws or a micrometer's faces gently and see that the scale reads zero; for a larger micrometer, use its setting rod. For a digital tool, check the battery and press the zero button with the jaws closed. Look at the calibration label to make sure the tool is in date. Check that the tool's range and resolution suit the job. If anything is wrong, do not use the tool; label it and report it.
markingPoints: Look for damage to jaws, faces, blades and scales
Moving parts move smoothly
Clean the faces
Check the zero (setting rod for larger micrometers; battery for digital tools)
Check calibration date and suitability; do not use a faulty tool, report it

essays.stem: Explain what a tolerance is, and describe how you would check that a batch of cut pieces is within tolerance.
essays.modelAnswer: A tolerance is the amount by which a size may vary from the size on the drawing and still be accepted. For example, 300 mm ± 1 mm means any piece from 299 mm to 301 mm is acceptable. To check a batch, I would first work out the smallest and largest sizes allowed and write them down. I would choose a measuring tool that reads finer than the tolerance, such as a steel rule or tape for ± 1 mm, or a vernier caliper for ± 0.1 mm, and check that it is in good order and reads zero. I would measure each piece the same way, from the same end, with the tool held square, and write each result in a table with the piece number. I would mark each piece that passes and put any piece that is outside the tolerance to one side, label it, and tell my supervisor.
markingPoints: Explains tolerance as allowed variation
Correct example of upper and lower limits
Chooses a tool finer than the tolerance and checks it
Measures each piece the same way and records results
Separates and labels pieces outside the tolerance and reports them

essays.stem: Explain why accurate measurement matters in both welding and fabrication and in electrical installation work. Give examples from both trades.
essays.modelAnswer: In welding and fabrication, parts must be cut and set to the right size so that they fit together. If a gate frame is measured wrongly, it will not fit the opening, the diagonals will not match and it may not swing or lock. A wrong root gap or bevel angle on a joint can give poor penetration and a weak weld. Wrong cutting wastes steel, which is costly. In electrical installation, cable and conduit runs must be measured so that there is enough length without waste. Outlets and switches must be fixed at the right heights and spacings, conduit must be bent to the right angles, and holes must be the right size for fittings. In both trades, accurate measurement saves time and material, makes the work safe and neat, and keeps the customer satisfied. It also means the work passes inspection the first time.
markingPoints: Welding example: fit-up, frame size or squareness
Welding example: joint gap or bevel affects weld quality
Electrical example: cable or conduit lengths
Electrical example: heights, spacing, bends or hole sizes
General benefits: saves material and time, safety, passes inspection

practical1.title: Measure a set of workshop parts with the right devices
practical1.brief: As a group, measure a set of numbered test pieces that the assessor provides, such as lengths of flat bar and round bar, a piece of plate with a bevelled edge, a short length of pipe or conduit, and a bolt. The assessor gives a measuring sheet listing the features to measure: lengths, widths, thicknesses, outside and inside diameters, a hole depth and a bevel angle. For each feature, the member choosing the device writes which tool they chose and why (tape, steel rule, vernier caliper, micrometer or protractor). Each member measures at least four features with at least three different devices, and records each reading with its unit. A second member then measures the same feature again to check it. Finally, the group compares its readings with the assessor's sizes and tolerances and marks each feature as within or outside tolerance. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the measuring sheet once for the whole group.
materials: Steel tape measure and 300 mm steel rule
Vernier caliper (0.02 mm) and 0–25 mm outside micrometer
Measuring sheet with sizes and tolerances
photos: The test pieces and measuring devices laid out and numbered
Each member taking a reading with a vernier caliper or micrometer (one photo per member)
A close-up of at least one vernier scale and one micrometer scale being read
A member measuring the bevel angle with the protractor
The completed measuring sheet showing both readings and the tolerance check
checklist: Chose a suitable device for each feature and gave a sensible reason
Cleaned the part and the device and checked the zero before measuring
Held the device square to the work with light, even pressure
Read the scale with the eye in line, without parallax error
Recorded each reading correctly with its unit
Re-measured another member's feature and agreed or corrected the reading
Judged correctly whether each feature was within tolerance
safety: Check test pieces for sharp edges and burrs; wear gloves to handle them and remove gloves to use precision tools
Keep precision devices on a cloth on the bench so that they cannot roll off and fall
Stand clear of any grinding or welding in the workshop; wear safety glasses if work is going on nearby

practical2.title: Check, clean, test and store a set of measuring devices
practical2.brief: As a group, carry out the maintenance check on a set of the workshop's graduated measuring devices, such as tape measures, steel rules, a square, vernier calipers and micrometers. Share the devices so that every member checks at least two. For each device: inspect it for damage, clean it, check that moving parts move smoothly, and check its zero. Check each vernier caliper and micrometer against a gauge block or setting rod of known size, and record the reading and the difference. Check each tape measure's hook and first 300 mm against a steel rule. Record every result on a device check register: the device, its condition, the zero and standard readings, the calibration label date, and whether it passes. Label any faulty or out-of-date device and set it aside. Finally, lightly oil the steel devices, close each micrometer with a small gap, and store every device in its case. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the register once for the whole group.
materials: A set of measuring devices from the workshop store
Gauge blocks or setting rods of known size
A 300 mm steel rule for checking tapes
Clean, soft cloths and a light machine oil
Device check register and faulty-device labels
The devices' cases or a padded drawer
photos: The devices laid out on a clean cloth before the check
Each member checking the zero of a vernier caliper or micrometer (one photo per member)
A device being checked against a gauge block or setting rod, with the reading visible
A tape measure's hook being checked against a steel rule
Any faulty device labelled and set aside, and the good devices oiled and stored in their cases
checklist: Inspected each device for damage and wear and reported what was found
Cleaned the faces and the scale with a soft cloth
Checked a device against a standard and recorded the difference correctly
Filled in the register clearly and correctly, including the calibration date
Labelled and set aside any faulty or out-of-date device
Oiled and stored the devices correctly, with micrometers left with a small gap
safety: Use only a little light oil, wipe up any drips, and wash hands afterwards
Handle gauge blocks with care: do not drop them or let them roll off the bench
Keep the work area tidy and the devices away from the edge of the bench
